questions.question: A disease has prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, and specificity 95%. What is P(disease | positive)?
questions.explanation: The true-positive mass is 0.01*0.90=0.009. False positives contribute 0.99*0.05=0.0495, so the posterior is 0.009/(0.0585), about 15.4%.

questions.question: A word appears zero times in a class with 10 observed tokens and vocabulary size 5. What does add-one Laplace smoothing give its probability?
questions.explanation: Add-one smoothing changes the numerator from 0 to 1 and the denominator from 10 to 10+5, preventing a single unseen word from making a whole document probability zero.

questions.question: How does a zero-mean Gaussian prior change MAP estimation compared with MLE?
options: It removes the likelihood and keeps only the prior mean
It forces every weight to exactly zero
It adds an L2 penalty that shrinks weights toward zero
It adds an L1 penalty and creates sparse coefficients
questions.explanation: Maximizing likelihood plus the log Gaussian prior adds a squared-weight penalty. That is the connection between MAP with a Gaussian prior and L2 regularization.

questions.question: Starting with Beta(1,1), what posterior follows from 3 successes and 1 failure?
questions.explanation: The Beta-Binomial update adds successes to alpha and failures to beta: (1+3, 1+1) = (4,2).

questions.question: Why does a Naive Bayes text classifier add log likelihoods for words?
options: Conditional independence turns a product into a sum in log space
Logarithms make every word equally likely
Adding logs removes the class prior from Bayes' rule
The classifier cannot represent probabilities below one
questions.explanation: The model multiplies conditional word probabilities under its independence assumption. Logs improve numerical stability and convert that product to a sum alongside log priors.

questions.question: The same positive test gives a lower posterior disease probability in a low-prevalence population than in a high-prevalence clinic. What changed?
options: The prior prevalence changed, so Bayes' posterior changed even with the same test
Specificity is irrelevant to positive results
The likelihood and prior are always interchangeable
questions.explanation: Bayes' denominator includes both true and false positives. Changing the base rate changes their mixture, which can substantially change the posterior.
